canonical_concept.beeja: यं (Yaṃ) — the bīja of vāyu (air/wind), the element most closely associated with prāṇa. Also हं (Haṃ) — the bīja of the throat chakra (Viśuddha) associated with prāṇa's vocal expression.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Prāṇa is a masculine noun. The prefix pra- (forward) combined with the root an- (to breathe) gives prāṇa — the primary, forward-moving life-breath. Distinguished from the five vāyus: Prāṇa (inward breath), Apāna (downward breath), Samāna (equalizing breath), Udāna (upward breath), Vyāna (pervading breath).
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Prāṇa is the universal life-force that animates all living beings. It operates through the prāṇamaya kosha (energy sheath) and the network of nāḍīs (energy channels). The five prāṇas (pañca-vāyu) govern specific physiological functions: Prāṇa (respiration, heart), Apāna (elimination, reproduction), Samāna (digestion, assimilation), Udāna (speech, upward movement, death), Vyāna (circulation, distribution). Prāṇāyāma (breath control) is the primary yogic practice for working with prāṇa.
canonical_concept.dhatu: प्र + अन् (Pra + An) — Pra (forward, forth) + An (to breathe, to live). That which breathes forth; the forward-moving breath.
canonical_concept.nirukta: "Prāṇiti iti prāṇaḥ" — that which breathes is prāṇa. The life-force that animates all living beings.
canonical_concept.tattva: Prāṇa-Tattva — the life-force principle. Prāṇa is the bridge between the physical body (annamaya kosha) and the mind (manomaya kosha). It is the animating principle that distinguishes the living from the dead.

The five prāṇas (pañca-vāyu) govern specific physiological functions: Prāṇa (respiration, heart), Apāna (elimination, reproduction), Samāna (digestion, assimilation), Udāna (speech, upward movement, death), Vyāna (circulation, distribution). provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In Vedic ontology: Prāṇa is the cosmic life-force — "prāṇo vai brahma" (Prāṇa is indeed Brahman — Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad). In Sāṃkhya: Prāṇa is the activity of the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra). In Advaita: Prāṇa is the manifestation of Brahman as the life-force. In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa — the governing principle of all movement and nervous function.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In Vedic cosmology: Prāṇa is the cosmic breath — the universe breathes in and out through cosmic cycles (kalpa). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad describes a cosmic debate among the prāṇas to determine which is supreme — prāṇa (breath) wins because when it leaves, all other faculties cease. In Purāṇic cosmology: Prāṇa is the breath of Brahma — the universe is created on his outbreath and dissolved on his inbreath.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In Yoga psychology: prāṇa and mind (manas) are intimately connected — "prāṇe manaḥ" (the mind is in prāṇa). Controlling prāṇa through prāṇāyāma controls the mind. The concept of prāṇa-spanda (the vibration of prāṇa) in Kashmir Śaivism is the basis of all mental activity. The five prāṇas govern different psychological functions: Prāṇa (attention, perception), Apāna (letting go, release), Samāna (integration, balance), Udāna (aspiration, will), Vyāna (expansion, connection).

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: The concept of prāṇa in governance: the king's prāṇa (vitality) is the prāṇa of the kingdom. The Arthaśāstra prescribes prāṇāyāma and yoga for the ruler's mental clarity. The concept of rāṣṭra-prāṇa (the life-force of the nation) appears in political philosophy.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In Āyurveda: Prāṇa is the primary vāta-doṣa governing the nervous system, respiration, and all movement. Prāṇa-vāyu specifically governs the heart and respiratory system. Prāṇa imbalance is the root of all vāta disorders. Prāṇāyāma is the primary Āyurvedic therapy for prāṇa disorders. The concept of prāṇa-pratīkāra (prāṇa therapy) includes breath work, marma therapy, and yoga.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: The concept of prāṇa in mathematics: the Vedic concept of prāṇa as the animating principle of numbers — each number has its own prāṇa (vitality). The concept of prāṇa in Vedic meter (chandas): each meter has a specific prāṇa (breath pattern) that gives it its power.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In Jyotiṣa: Prāṇa is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic prāṇa-source. The concept of prāṇa-āyuṣa (life-span calculation) in Jyotiṣa uses prāṇa as the unit of time. The prāṇa (a unit of time = 4 seconds) is the smallest unit in Vedic time measurement.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: In alchemical traditions: prāṇa is the life-force that must be infused into alchemical preparations. The concept of prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) in idol-making is the ritual infusion of prāṇa into a metal image. Mercury (pārada) is considered the prāṇa of metals in Rasaśāstra.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: Prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā (installation of life-force) is the ritual that animates a deity's image. The prāṇāyāma performed before ritual purifies the prāṇa of the practitioner. The concept of prāṇa-āhuti (offering of prāṇa) in yajña — the breath itself is offered to the fire.

provenance.source_text: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1-14 (the debate of the prāṇas)

claims.value: The breath symbolizes prāṇa — the most immediate experience of life-force. The wind (vāyu) symbolizes prāṇa's invisible, pervading nature. The serpent (nāga) symbolizes prāṇa's movement through the nāḍīs. The lotus symbolizes prāṇa's blooming in the heart.
